usage: Sentence-initial contrast, more formal than 하지만
Pairs naturally with the plain written ending -다 in reports
Dramatic reversal in essays and narration
Marks an unexpected turn in a written account
examples: 좋은 생각이에요. 그러나 돈이 없어요.
It's a good idea. However, there's no money.
Simple two-sentence flip; 그러나 always opens the second sentence
회사는 빠르게 성장했어요. 그러나 직원들은 더 힘들어졌어요.
The company grew fast. However, the employees had it harder.
Report or news-style contrast between two facts
여러 번 시도했지만 모두 실패했다. 그러나 그는 멈추지 않았다.
He tried many times but failed every time. However, he did not stop.
Narrative register: note the bookish -다 ending matching 그러나's tone
nuance: 그러나 means 'however' and is the formal, written-register cousin of 하지만 and 그렇지만. Its dividing line from those: 하지만 is the neutral all-purpose 'but' that works in speech and writing, while 그러나 feels distinctly literary and shows up in news articles, reports, essays, editorials, and official notices; in casual chat it sounds stiff, where 근데 or 하지만 fit far better. A second crucial point for English speakers: 그러나 almost always STARTS a fresh sentence and does not glue two clauses together inside one sentence. English 'but' can sit mid-sentence ('I tried, but I failed'), so learners wrongly write 시도했어요 그러나 실패했어요; correct Korean either puts 그러나 after a full stop or uses the clause-internal ending -지만 (시도했지만 실패했어요). Treat 그러나 as a heading-level pivot, not an inline conjunction.

Pairing it with the casual 요-ending in formal writing; 그러나 normally goes with the plain -다 style (그러나 결과는 달랐다)

english: then, in that case, if so
usage: Then let's do it this way
Drawing a next step from what was just said
In that case it won't do / you mustn't
그러면 안 되다 is a fixed 'that's not allowed' phrase
Settling a plan based on the prior point
Asking for the next move given the situation
examples: 배고파요? 그러면 라면 끓일게요.
You're hungry? Then I'll make ramyeon.
Simple condition-then-action; reacts to what the other person said
이 서류가 필요해요. 그러면 먼저 주민센터에 가야 해요.
You need this document. In that case, you have to go to the community center first.
Chains a required step to a stated need
다들 동의해요? 그럼 이대로 진행할게요.
Does everyone agree? Then I'll proceed as is.
Shows the everyday contraction 그럼 in real conversation
nuance: 그러면 means 'then / in that case' and links a conclusion or next step to a condition that was just stated, with the logic 'if that's the situation, then this.' It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + -면 ('if'), so literally it is 'if it is so' — keeping that origin in mind explains why it always reacts to a premise. In fast speech it contracts to 그럼, which is identical in meaning and is what you'll actually hear most of the time. The key contrast for learners is against 그리고: 그러면 responds to a CONDITION ('if so, then...'), whereas 그리고 simply lists the NEXT EVENT in time ('and then'). So 'I woke up and then ate' is 일어났어요. 그리고 먹었어요 — using 그러면 there is wrong because nothing is conditional. Note too that the lookalike 그러면서 ('while doing so') is a different word and not a contraction of this one.

english: so, that's why, what I mean is
usage: 그러니까 내 말이 is a strong 'I totally agree' phrase
That's why I told you to be careful
Stating the logical takeaway as advice
So, what do you mean by that?
Filler-like use to reorganize or push a thought
examples: 비 온대요. 그러니까 우산 챙겨요.
They say it'll rain. So bring an umbrella.
Simple: derives a piece of advice from a fact
주말엔 사람이 많아요. 그러니까 평일에 가는 게 나아요.
Weekends are crowded. That's why going on a weekday is better.
Gives the reasoning behind a recommendation
그러니까 제 말은, 지금 결정하지 말자는 거예요.
What I mean is, let's not decide right now.
그러니까 제 말은 restates and clarifies your own point
nuance: 그러니까 means 'so / that's why' and presents what follows as the reason-driven result of what came before. It comes from 그렇다 + -(으)니까 ('because it is so'), and that -니까 root is the key to its flavor: -니까 is the 'because' that naturally leads into commands, requests, and urging, which is exactly why 그러니까 pairs so well with advice (일찍 자요) and 'I-told-you-so' lines. This is the sharp dividing line from near-synonym 그래서: 그래서 (from 그렇다 + -아서) merely REPORTS a result neutrally ('so, as a result'), and crucially 그래서 cannot head a command, while 그러니까 actively REASONS and PERSUADES and happily does. Beyond logic, 그러니까 is a heavy conversational filler — 그러니까 내 말이 means 'exactly, that's my point!' (strong agreement), and a trailing 그러니까... works like English 'I mean...' when you restate yourself. English speakers who treat it as a plain synonym of 그래서 miss both the urging nuance and these idiomatic uses.

english: on top of that, moreover, what's more
usage: And on top of that, it's expensive
Piling on one more (often negative) point
What's more, even the weather is bad
On top of that, it's free
Adding a further positive selling point
Plus, the place is close too
examples: 이 식당 맛있어요. 게다가 싸요.
This restaurant is tasty. On top of that, it's cheap.
Simple: stacks a second perk in the same positive direction
야근을 했어요. 게다가 막차까지 놓쳤어요.
I worked overtime. On top of that, I even missed the last train.
게다가 ~까지 piling on a worse second misfortune
방이 넓어요. 게다가 월세도 싸서 바로 계약했어요.
The room is spacious. Plus the rent is cheap too, so I signed right away.
게다가 ~도 reinforcing a decision with an added reason
nuance: 게다가 means 'on top of that / moreover / what's more,' adding a second point that pushes in the SAME direction as the first — two good things or two bad things stacking up to intensify the overall impression. Its defining contrast is with neutral 그리고 ('and'): 그리고 simply lists items with no emotional slope ('A and B'), while 게다가 conveys 'and as if that weren't enough, also B,' so swapping in a flat 그리고 throws away the cumulative punch. It habitually teams up with the particles 까지 ('even') and 도 ('also') on the added item — 게다가 비까지 와요 ('and on top of that it's even raining'), 게다가 집도 가까워요 — and learning that 게다가 ... 까지/도 frame is the fastest way to sound natural. The big English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 게다가 to add a CONTRASTING point ('it's expensive, however...'); 게다가 cannot pivot, so a contrast needs 하지만 or 그런데 instead.

Forgetting the partner particles; natural 게다가 sentences usually carry 까지 or 도 on the added element (게다가 날씨까지 안 좋아요)

usage: Draws a formal consequence in a notice (with -ㅂ니다)
Therefore, it may be subject to change
examples: 오늘은 휴일입니다. 따라서 은행은 문을 닫습니다.
Today is a holiday. Therefore the bank is closed.
Simple formal cause-effect, paired with -ㅂ니다 style
서류가 미비합니다. 따라서 접수가 어렵습니다.
The documents are incomplete. Accordingly, we cannot accept the application.
Administrative, official register
규정이 바뀌었습니다. 따라서 모두 다시 신청하셔야 합니다.
The rules have changed. Therefore, everyone must reapply.
Announcing a required consequence in a notice
nuance: 따라서 means 'therefore / accordingly / thus' and is the formal, logical 'so' of reports, public notices, instructions, contracts, and academic writing. It states a conclusion that follows STRICTLY and objectively from the prior statement, with a more official, impersonal tone than either 그래서 (plain spoken 'so') or 그러니까 (reasoning/urging 'so'). The dividing line: 그래서 and 그러니까 belong to everyday speech and can carry personal feeling or persuasion, whereas 따라서 is detached and rule-like, so in casual conversation it sounds like you're reading a press release. It pairs naturally with the formal -ㅂ니다 ending and with 다음과 같이 ('as follows'). The classic English-speaker trap is mixing this connector up with the homograph verb form 따라서 from 따르다 ('to follow') — as in 규칙을 따라서 ('following the rule'). The connector stands ALONE at the head of a sentence with no object; the verb form has something being followed in front of it.

english: on the other hand, whereas, by contrast
usage: On the other hand, there are downsides too
Introducing the opposite side of a point
By contrast, the price is high
Weighing a drawback against an upside
As a clause ending -는/은 반면에, attached directly to a verb/adjective
examples: 형은 키가 커요. 반면에 저는 작아요.
My older brother is tall. By contrast, I'm short.
Simple A-vs-B contrast of two clearly stated sides
도시는 편리해요. 반면에 집값이 너무 비싸요.
Cities are convenient. On the other hand, housing is way too expensive.
Balancing one pro against one con
월급은 늘어난 반면에 일은 훨씬 많아졌어요.
While the salary went up, the workload grew much more.
Shows the bound form -ㄴ 반면에 joining the two sides in one sentence
nuance: 반면에 means 'on the other hand / whereas / by contrast' and explicitly sets two distinct sides, options, or qualities against each other. It comes from the Sino-Korean noun 반면 (反面, literally 'opposite + face/side,' i.e. 'the reverse side') plus the location particle 에 — so its very composition is 'on the opposite side,' which is why it demands a clear A and a clear B to weigh. This is its dividing line from 그런데/근데: those handle a single-topic surprise or twist ('I went out, but it was closed'), whereas 반면에 is analytical and comparative, ideal for pros-and-cons and 'A is X, B is Y' contrasts. It also differs from 한편 in being a sharper head-to-head contrast rather than a loose scene-shift. Note it has two shapes: as a free adverb starting a sentence (반면에 단점도 있어요) and as a bound clause ending -는/은 반면에 attached to the previous verb/adjective (비싼 반면에 'while it's expensive'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping it onto a one-sided remark where there's no real B to contrast — without two sides, 반면에 has nothing to balance and sounds incomplete.

english: that is, in other words, namely
usage: That is, to put it another way
In other words, it means it's free
즉 ...라는 거예요 spells out what something amounts to
Cutting straight to the core point
examples: 이건 보증금이에요. 즉, 나중에 돌려받는 돈이에요.
This is a deposit. That is, money you get back later.
Restates a term in plainer words; note the comma after 즉
오늘은 공휴일이에요. 즉, 관공서는 다 쉬어요.
Today is a public holiday. In other words, all government offices are closed.
Draws the practical implication of a fact
계약이 끝났어요. 즉, 이제 다른 집을 구해야 한다는 거죠.
The contract ended. That is, it means I now have to find another place.
즉 ...라는 거죠 reframing a fact as its real consequence
nuance: 즉 means 'that is / in other words / namely' and introduces a RESTATEMENT or precise clarification of what you just said — never new information, only the same point re-expressed more sharply or simply. It is a single Sino-Korean syllable from the hanja 卽 ('namely, that is to say'), and that one-syllable crispness gives it a slightly formal, definitional ring that suits writing, explanations, legal/technical text, and definitions. The contrast to watch: do not confuse 즉 with 그리고 ('and'), which ADDS a separate item; 즉 re-explains, so if what follows is genuinely new content, 즉 is wrong. It overlaps heavily with 다시 말해 ('in other words'), but 즉 is terser and more bookish while 다시 말해 feels more conversational. Punctuation-wise it almost always takes a comma right after it (즉,) and pairs naturally with the nominalizing tails ...라는 거예요 / ...뜻이에요. In very casual chat it can feel clipped, where 그러니까 or 말하자면 sound friendlier.

english: in other words, to put it differently
usage: In other words, it means no
Rephrasing to make the point unmistakable
다시 말해서 is the equally common longer form
In other words, it means there's no money
Put differently, it means there isn't enough time
examples: 보증금이 비싸요. 다시 말해, 초기 비용이 많이 들어요.
The deposit is high. In other words, the upfront cost is large.
Reframes the point in clearer everyday terms
답장이 없어요. 다시 말해, 거절이라는 뜻이죠.
There's no reply. In other words, it means a rejection.
Interprets the real meaning behind a fact
예약이 다 찼어요. 다시 말해서 오늘은 자리가 없어요.
Reservations are full. To put it another way, there are no seats today.
Shows the interchangeable longer form 다시 말해서
nuance: 다시 말해 literally breaks down as 다시 ('again') + 말해 (the connective form of 말하다, 'to speak'), so its bones say 'speaking again,' working exactly like English 'in other words.' It introduces a clearer, blunter, or more interpretive rephrasing of what you just said, and the fuller form 다시 말해서 is just as common and fully interchangeable. Its near-twin is 즉: both restate, but 다시 말해 is a touch more conversational and explanatory in feel, whereas 즉 is terser and more bookish — so when softly walking a listener through a confusing point, 다시 말해 sounds warmer. The pitfall for English speakers is the surface resemblance to the plain verb phrase 다시 말하다 meaning 'to say (it) again' i.e. to literally repeat the same words; 다시 말해 as a connector does NOT mean verbatim repetition — it signals a reworded explanation, the same idea recast, not the identical sentence said twice.

usage: Giving a concrete instance of a category
예를 들어서 is the equally natural longer form
예를 들면 is a common interchangeable variant
예를 들다 used as a full verb, 'to raise an example'
examples: 한국 음식 좋아해요. 예를 들어 떡볶이요.
I like Korean food. For example, tteokbokki.
Simple: one concrete instance of a stated preference
서류가 좀 필요해요. 예를 들어 외국인등록증 같은 거요.
You need some documents. For example, things like your residence card.
예를 들어 ... 같은 거 clarifies a vague category with a sample
취미가 많아요. 예를 들어 등산도 하고 사진도 찍어요.
I have many hobbies. For example, I hike and take photos.
Introducing illustrative activities, here with 도 ... 도
nuance: 예를 들어 means 'for example / for instance' and is the everyday way to introduce a concrete case of a general statement. It is built from the Sino-Korean noun 예 (例, 'example') plus the verb 들다 here meaning 'to raise/cite,' so it literally reads 'raising an example' — the same 들다 as in 손을 들다 ('raise one's hand'). Because it is genuinely a verb phrase, you can flex it: 예를 들어 볼게요 ('let me give an example'), 예를 들어서 (longer connective form), or 예를 들면 ('if one takes an example'), all natural and interchangeable. It works in every register, from chat to academic writing, which makes it one of the most reliable connectors for explaining yourself. The English-speaker pitfalls are two spelling traps: never close up the space (the standard is 예를 들어, not 예를들어), and never blend the variant endings into the non-word 예를 들어면 — the valid forms are 예를 들어 / 예를 들어서 / 예를 들면 only.

Pluralizing it like English 'examples'; Korean keeps the singular 예 here, e.g. 예를 들어, not 예들을 들어

usage: 그럼에도 불구하고 is the set, emphatic full form
Even so, I didn't give up
Sticking to a decision against the odds
Even so, the result was good
examples: 힘들었어요. 그럼에도 끝까지 했어요.
It was hard. Even so, I finished it to the end.
Simple: persistence despite a stated difficulty
월급이 적어요. 그럼에도 이 일을 계속하는 이유가 있어요.
The pay is low. Nevertheless, there's a reason I keep this job.
Introduces a clause that defies expectation
몸이 안 좋았어요. 그럼에도 불구하고 행사를 진행했어요.
I wasn't feeling well. In spite of that, I went ahead with the event.
The full emphatic 그럼에도 불구하고 in a weightier register
nuance: 그럼에도 means 'even so / nevertheless / despite that' and signals that what follows happens AGAINST the obstacle just mentioned. It is built from 그렇다 ('to be so') + the concessive ending -ㅁ에도 ('even though it is'), so structurally it is 'even though it is so.' It is most often heard in its set full form 그럼에도 불구하고 ('in spite of that' — 불구하고 from 不拘, 'not being bound by'), which adds gravity and is common in speeches, editorials, and formal writing. The dividing line to learn is against everyday 그래도: 그래도 is the casual, neutral 'still / even so' you use with friends, while 그럼에도 carries an elevated, determined, slightly dramatic tone — choosing 그럼에도 in a light chat sounds like you've suddenly switched to a TED talk. So the English-speaker pitfall is register mismatch: reach for 그래도 in conversation and reserve 그럼에도 (불구하고) for emphatic or written contexts. Also memorize the fixed spelling 불구하고 — not the common mishearing 불구하구.

english: meanwhile, on the other hand, for one's part
usage: Shifting the scene to a parallel situation
한편으로는 introduces one of two mixed feelings
At the same time, I was also worried
on one hand ~ on the other hand
The paired frame for two simultaneous sides
examples: 저는 신났어요. 한편 부모님은 걱정하셨어요.
I was excited. Meanwhile, my parents were worried.
Simple: shifts to a parallel, contrasting reaction
한편으로는 기쁘고, 한편으로는 아쉬워요.
On one hand I'm happy, and on the other I'm a little sad.
The doubled 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는 frame for mixed feelings
회사는 채용을 줄였어요. 한편 업무량은 더 늘었어요.
The company cut hiring. Meanwhile, the workload only grew.
News-style topic shift to a parallel development
nuance: 한편 means 'meanwhile / on the other hand / for one's part' and shifts attention to a PARALLEL or co-existing situation rather than flatly contradicting the first. It is Sino-Korean, 한 (一, 'one') + 편 (便/篇, 'side'), literally 'one side' — so it frames the next thing as 'one side of the picture,' which is why it can introduce a simultaneous scene, not just an opposite. In news writing, a bare 한편, ... is the standard way to switch topics ('In other news, ...'). Its near-synonym is 반면에, and the dividing line matters: 반면에 (反面, 'opposite side') is a SHARP head-to-head A-vs-B contrast for weighing pros and cons, whereas 한편 is looser and more reportorial, often just panning the camera to a parallel event or adding a coexisting angle. Its most useful conversational life is the doubled frame 한편으로는 ~ 한편으로는 (또는 다른 한편으로는), meaning 'part of me... but part of me...,' for mixed feelings. The English pitfall is treating 한편 as a plain 'but'; it does not negate the first clause, it sets a second view beside it.

english: in the end, eventually, after all
usage: In the end, I couldn't go
Reporting how things finally turned out
It ended up like this after all
In the end it'll all work out
결국엔 adds 은 to stress the final outcome
A final result reached after a struggle
examples: 고민하다가 결국 안 샀어요.
I kept hesitating and in the end didn't buy it.
Simple: marks the final decision after wavering
며칠을 버텼지만 결국 병원에 갔어요.
I held out for days, but I eventually went to the hospital.
Outcome reached after resistance; note the lead-in -지만
다들 말렸는데 결국 제 뜻대로 했어요.
Everyone tried to stop me, but in the end I did it my way.
Stresses the eventual result despite opposition, with -는데
nuance: 결국 means 'in the end / eventually / after all' and sums up the FINAL outcome reached after a process, delay, or struggle. It is Sino-Korean, 결 (結, 'to conclude/tie up') + 국 (局, 'situation/end stage'), literally 'the concluding stage' — so it inherently looks back over a whole drawn-out affair to its settling point. The dividing line from near-synonym 드디어 is important: 드디어 celebrates a happy, long-awaited result with relief and excitement ('finally, at last!'), whereas 결국 is emotionally NEUTRAL and frequently tinged with resignation or a sense that the outcome was inevitable ('it came to this after all'). A second contrast English speakers stumble on: 결국 is NOT the 'finally/lastly' that orders items in a list — that ordinal sense ('firstly... finally...') is 마지막으로. 결국 is about how a story RESOLVED, not where an item sits in a sequence. It commonly follows a lead-in clause with -지만 or -는데 sketching the struggle, and the variant 결국엔 (with topic 은) adds extra weight to the final beat.
